content: The ABCC1 gene encodes a protein known as Multidrug Resistance-Associated Protein 1 (MRP1) in humans. This protein belongs to the ATP-binding cassette (ABC) transporter superfamily, which is responsible for transporting various molecules across both extracellular and intracellular membranes. ABC genes are categorized into seven subfamilies: ABC1, MDR/TAP, MRP, ALD, OABP, GCN20, and White. MRP1 is a member of the MRP subfamily, which is associated with multidrug resistance. It functions as a multispecific organic anion transporter, with substrates including oxidized glutathione, cysteinyl leukotrienes, and activated aflatoxin B1. Additionally, it transports glucuronides and sulfate conjugates of steroid hormones and bile salts. Alternative splicing of the ABCC1 gene, involving exon deletion, results in several splice variants, all of which retain the original open reading frame. The ABCC1 protein is a 190 kDa molecule composed of two hydrophobic membrane-spanning domains and two nucleotide-binding domains. Each membrane-spanning domain consists of six α-helices. A unique feature of ABCC1 is the presence of a third membrane-spanning domain, distinguishing it from other ABC transporters. The two nucleotide-binding domains exhibit functional asymmetry, which is critical for ATP-driven transport. The first domain, NBD1, is responsible for strong ATP binding, while the second domain, NBD2, facilitates ATP hydrolysis. This asymmetry is specific to the C subfamily of ABC transporters and is not observed in other transporter families. The ABCC1 gene is highly conserved, with polymorphisms occurring at low frequencies (less than 5%), typically in the form of single-nucleotide polymorphisms (SNPs). Ethnic differences in polymorphisms are notable, with variations observed between Caucasian and Asian populations. Some SNPs are shared among Asian populations but absent in Caucasians, and vice versa. The ABCC1 gene is located on chromosome 16 within the nucleus. The protein is intracellularly localized on the basolateral side of the plasma membrane, unlike other ABC transporters, which are typically found on the apical side. ABCC1 is expressed in most human tissues but is particularly abundant in the lungs, spleen, testes, kidneys, placenta, thyroid, bladder, and adrenal glands. It is also present in the endothelial cells of the blood-brain barrier. Certain polymorphisms in the ABCC1 gene are associated with an increased susceptibility to specific cancers. For example, the G2168A polymorphism and variants in the 3'-UTR region of the gene are linked to a higher risk of lung cancer, particularly in Chinese populations. Carriers of the G2168A polymorphism have a nearly fourfold increased risk of developing lung cancer compared to individuals without the mutation. Polymorphisms in ABCC1 also influence the severity of diseases such as cystic fibrosis (CF) and chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD). In CF, individuals with a G-260C polymorphism in the 5'-UTR region of ABCC1 tend to experience more severe disease compared to those with the wild-type gene. In COPD, the presence of a 3'-UTR T866A polymorphism is associated with less severe disease and reduced airway inflammation, whereas the 3'-UTR G3361A polymorphism correlates with more severe disease and increased airway inflammation. The ABCC1 protein has garnered attention for its potential role in Alzheimer’s disease (AD). A hallmark of AD is the accumulation of β-amyloid proteins in the brain, which form plaques that disrupt neural signaling. Due to its localization in the choroid plexus and blood-brain barrier, as well as its ability to transport various molecules out of cells, ABCC1 has been studied extensively in the context of AD. Activation of ABCC1 has been shown to reduce β-amyloid accumulation by nearly 80%, making it a promising target for future treatments of AD and other neurological disorders. In cancer, ABCC1 contributes to multidrug resistance in tumor cells by transporting chemotherapeutic drugs out of the cells. High expression of ABCC1 is particularly prevalent in neuroblastoma and cancers of the lung, breast, and prostate. In non-small cell lung carcinoma and small cell lung carcinoma, elevated ABCC1 expression is associated with reduced responsiveness to chemotherapy and lower survival rates. Similarly, in early-stage breast cancer, increased ABCC1 expression correlates with shorter relapse times and decreased survival. In prostate cancer, ABCC1 expression increases with disease progression and confers resistance to chemotherapy. Animal studies have highlighted the importance of ABCC1 in the transport of organic anion molecules and its association with various diseases, including AD. In ABCC1 knockout mice, β-amyloid clearance is significantly reduced compared to wild-type mice. In mouse models of AD, treatment with thiethylperazine, a drug that activates ABCC1, enhances β-amyloid clearance and reduces its accumulation in the brain. St. John’s wort, which contains the compound hyperforin, has also been shown to positively influence ABCC1 activity. In a study involving APP-tg mice, an extract of St. John’s wort with reduced hyperforin levels increased ABCC1 activity by 70%, leading to decreased β-amyloid levels in the brain and improved cognitive function in the mice. Interactive pathway maps allow researchers to explore the relationships between genes, proteins, and metabolites, providing valuable insights into the functional roles of ABCC1 in health and disease.
